title: Graph Theory Basics
tagline: Vertices, edges, and the elegant theorems connecting them: graph theory is the mathematical backbone of networks, routing, scheduling, and social systems.

sections.content:
A **graph** G = (V, E) consists of a set of **vertices** (nodes) V and a set of **edges** E connecting pairs of vertices. Graphs model an astonishing range of real-world systems: the internet (servers and links), social networks (people and friendships), compilers (variables and dependencies), maps (intersections and roads), and CPU scheduling (tasks and conflicts). The same mathematical framework — vertices and edges — handles all of these.

Graphs can be **undirected** (edges have no direction: friendship is mutual) or **directed** (digraphs: edges are arrows, like a one-way street or a dependency). They can be **weighted** (each edge has a cost or capacity) or **unweighted**. Key questions graph theory answers: Is there a path between two nodes? What is the shortest path? Can we colour nodes so no two adjacent nodes share a colour? Does an Euler circuit (visit every edge once) exist? These questions translate directly to routing protocols, register allocation, and network flow.

sections.title: Cities and Roads, Handshakes and Degrees
sections.content:
Think of a graph as a map of cities connected by roads. The **degree** of a city is the number of roads directly connected to it. The **handshaking lemma** says the total number of handshakes at a party equals twice the number of pairs who shook hands — because each handshake is counted by both participants. In graph terms: the sum of all degrees equals twice the number of edges. A surprising corollary: every graph has an even number of odd-degree vertices.

A **path** is a journey between cities without repeating a city. A **cycle** returns to the starting city. A **tree** is a map where there is exactly one path between any two cities — no cycles, no alternative routes. Cut one road and the map disconnects; add one road and you create a cycle. **Connectivity** is about reachability: can you drive from city A to city B at all?

**Degree and handshaking lemma**: in an undirected graph, deg(v) is the number of edges incident to vertex v. The handshaking lemma states Σ deg(v) = 2|E|. This implies the number of odd-degree vertices is always even. In a directed graph, each vertex has in-degree (edges pointing in) and out-degree (edges pointing out); Σ in-degree = Σ out-degree = |E|.

**Paths and cycles**: a **walk** visits vertices with possible repetition; a **path** visits each vertex at most once; a **cycle** is a closed path (start = end). A graph is **connected** if there exists a path between every pair of vertices. A **connected component** is a maximal connected subgraph. A graph without any cycle is **acyclic** (or a **forest**). A connected acyclic graph is a **tree** — trees have exactly |V| − 1 edges.

**Euler paths and circuits**: an **Eulerian circuit** visits every edge exactly once and returns to the start. Euler's theorem: a connected graph has an Eulerian circuit if and only if every vertex has even degree. An **Eulerian path** (not necessarily a circuit) exists if and only if exactly two vertices have odd degree (those are the endpoints). This is why you can draw certain shapes without lifting your pen.

**Hamiltonian paths and cycles**: a **Hamiltonian path** visits every vertex exactly once (not every edge). Unlike Euler, no simple characterisation exists — determining if a Hamiltonian cycle exists is NP-complete. This is essentially the Travelling Salesman Problem.

**Graph colouring**: a **k-colouring** assigns one of k colours to each vertex such that no two adjacent vertices share a colour. The **chromatic number** χ(G) is the minimum k needed. Trees are always 2-colourable (bipartite). Planar graphs need at most 4 colours (four-colour theorem). Colouring models register allocation in compilers, scheduling, and exam timetabling.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: The adjacency list uses a Map for O(1) vertex lookup. BFS computes shortest path distances in an unweighted graph by exploring level by level. The Euler circuit check counts odd-degree vertices: graph g has vertices B(degree 3) and C(degree 3) with odd degree — exactly 2 odd-degree vertices, meaning it has an Eulerian PATH (A→B→D→E→C→A? — actually tracing confirms it) but not an Eulerian circuit. The handshaking lemma: sum=12=2×6 edges confirmed.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Trees are graphs with exactly |V|−1 edges and no cycles.** Any two of the three properties (connected, acyclic, |E|=|V|−1) imply the third for finite graphs — so you only need to verify two. **BFS gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs** (O(V+E)); add weights and use Dijkstra. For Eulerian circuits, check degrees in O(V+E) — no need to trace the circuit. For Hamiltonian cycles, no polynomial check exists — it is NP-complete. Bipartite graphs are exactly those with no odd cycles; BFS 2-colouring detects them in O(V+E).

items: A **graph** G=(V,E) models relationships; edges can be undirected/directed, weighted/unweighted. **Adjacency lists** give O(V+E) space and are standard for sparse graphs.
**Handshaking lemma**: Σ deg(v) = 2|E|; the number of odd-degree vertices is always even. In digraphs, Σ in-degree = Σ out-degree = |E|.
**Trees** are connected acyclic graphs with exactly |V|−1 edges; any two of {connected, acyclic, |E|=|V|−1} imply the third.
**Eulerian circuit** exists iff the graph is connected and all vertices have even degree; **Eulerian path** exists iff exactly two vertices have odd degree. Hamiltonian cycle is NP-complete.

**Graph colouring** assigns colours to vertices so adjacent vertices differ; χ(G) is the chromatic number. Trees are bipartite (2-colourable); planarity and structural theorems bound χ for special graph classes.

quiz.question: A graph has 5 vertices with degrees 2, 3, 3, 4, 4. How many edges does it have?
quiz.explanation: By the handshaking lemma: Σ deg(v) = 2|E|. Sum of degrees = 2+3+3+4+4 = 16. So |E| = 16/2 = 8.

quiz.question: A connected graph with n vertices that is also acyclic (no cycles) must have how many edges?
quiz.explanation: A connected acyclic graph is a tree. Trees have exactly n−1 edges. This is because you need at least n−1 edges for connectivity (a spanning tree), and adding any edge to a tree creates exactly one cycle — so acyclicity caps it at n−1.

quiz.question: Which condition guarantees an Eulerian circuit exists in a connected undirected graph?
options: Exactly two vertices have odd degree
quiz.explanation: Euler's theorem: a connected undirected graph has an Eulerian circuit (visiting every edge exactly once and returning to start) if and only if every vertex has even degree. Exactly two odd-degree vertices gives an Eulerian path (not circuit) with those vertices as endpoints.

quiz.question: BFS (Breadth-First Search) from a source vertex gives:
options: Shortest paths by edge count in weighted graphs
Shortest paths by edge count in unweighted graphs
quiz.explanation: BFS explores vertices level by level, so vertices at BFS distance d are reachable in exactly d edges. This gives shortest paths by hop count in unweighted graphs. For weighted graphs you need Dijkstra (non-negative weights) or Bellman-Ford (negative weights). Topological sort uses DFS on DAGs.

quiz.question: A digraph (directed graph) with |V|=5 and |E|=8 has Σ in-degrees equal to:
quiz.explanation: In a directed graph, each edge contributes exactly 1 to some vertex's in-degree and 1 to some vertex's out-degree. Therefore Σ in-degree = Σ out-degree = |E| = 8. The sum of degrees (in+out) = 2|E| = 16.

quiz.question: Is determining whether a graph has a Hamiltonian cycle computationally easy (polynomial)?
options: Yes — check if all vertices have degree ≥ 2
Yes — use a modified DFS in O(V+E)
No — it is NP-complete; no polynomial algorithm is known
Yes — it reduces to checking Eulerian conditions
quiz.explanation: The Hamiltonian cycle problem is NP-complete — no polynomial-time algorithm is known (and none is expected unless P=NP). Unlike Eulerian circuits (polynomial via degree check), Hamiltonian cycles have no simple structural characterisation. Dirac's theorem gives sufficient conditions but not necessary ones.

quiz.question: A bipartite graph can always be coloured with at most how many colours?
quiz.explanation: A bipartite graph has vertices split into two sets U, V such that all edges go between U and V (none within). Colour all of U with colour 1, all of V with colour 2 — no two adjacent vertices share a colour. Bipartite = 2-colourable = contains no odd-length cycles. Trees are a special case of bipartite graphs.

quiz.question: The handshaking lemma implies which surprising fact about any graph?
options: Every graph must have at least one vertex of degree 0
The number of vertices with odd degree is always even
The sum of degrees equals the number of vertices
quiz.explanation: Since Σ deg(v) = 2|E| (an even number), and the even-degree vertices contribute an even sum, the odd-degree vertices must collectively sum to something even — which requires an even count of them. This means you can never have exactly 1, 3, or 5 odd-degree vertices in any graph.

quiz.question: What is the minimum number of colours needed to colour a tree (chromatic number)?
options: 2 (for any tree with at least one edge)
It depends on the maximum degree
quiz.explanation: All trees are bipartite — they contain no odd cycles (in fact no cycles at all). Bipartite graphs are exactly the 2-colourable graphs. So any tree with at least one edge needs exactly 2 colours. A single isolated vertex needs only 1 colour, but any tree with edges needs 2.

quiz.question: In a directed acyclic graph (DAG), which algorithm produces a valid linear ordering of vertices respecting all edge directions?
options: Topological sort via DFS or Kahn's algorithm
quiz.explanation: Topological sort produces a linear ordering of vertices such that for every directed edge u→v, u appears before v. It is only defined for DAGs (cycles make total ordering impossible). DFS-based topological sort adds vertices to a stack in post-order; Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes vertices with in-degree 0. Both run in O(V+E).
